extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, government contracting officers, procurement officials, and legal scholars studying government contract law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing formation, modification, waiver, and enforcement of United States government contracts, with emphasis on bids, mistakes, delegated authority, consideration for modifications, specifications, and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineer approval binds parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a contract which provides that stone to be furnished by the contractor must be 'sandstone of quality approved by the engineer,' the decision of the engineer binds the Government as well as the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Barlow v. United States (35 Ct. Cls., 514). Use when contract language vests approval in an engineer; his decision is binding on both contractor and government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superior officer exceeding contract terms not binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract prescribes 'sandstone of a quality approved by the engineer,' and the superior officer who entered into the contract requires 'the best sandstone which can be obtained,' the stone required is not the stone contracted for, and the contractor can recover for the difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an officer imposes a higher standard than the contract, contractor may recover difference; distinguish between authorized engineer approvals and unilateral higher demands by superior officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval by higher officer does not compel delegated official
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the engineer in charge is authorized by the contract to extend the time for performance, the fact that the Chief of Engineers approves of his extending it to a day specified does not compel him to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Kennedy v. United States (24 Ct. Cls., 122). Delegated discretion remains with the delegatee; higher approval does not retroactively alter delegated decision-making duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving officer's charge subject to commander approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract provides that the receiving officer may charge the contractor with loss resulting from neglect to deliver at the prescribed time, subject, however, to the approval of the department commander, the contractor is entitled to have exercised the discretion of the receiving officer and the department commander, and is not bound by the action of the receiving officer who is ordered by the post commander to make the charge and in obedience to the order does so without the approval of the department commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Baldwin. When contract conditions require multi-level approvals, contractor can insist on proper exercise of discretion by required approvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: No power to release or increase compensation without consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: You have no authority to absolve a contractor from his obligation to do the work; and, if he does it, you cannot authorize him to be paid for it at higher price than the contract stipulates for. You can not relieve him from hardship either by giving damages, releasing him from his present contract, or by making a new one, without proper authority or consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion: Attorney General Black. Relief (release or increased pay) requires statutory or other authority and adequate consideration; absent breach by the United States, officers cannot unilaterally grant such relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification releasing contractor requires real, substantial consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A new contract releasing a contractor from forfeiture could be legally made only upon a consideration that is real, substantial, and not imaginary, or one not growing out of or based wholly upon the failure in performance of the original contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: V Comp. Dec. and related authorities. Consideration must benefit the United States and be independent and adequate to support a waiver or release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers lack plenary power to waive time if detrimental to Government
rubrics_metrics.description: A Government officer is not authorized to extend the time of a contract if such extension will operate to release the contractor or his sureties from liability for damages or be otherwise detrimental to the interests of the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VIII Comp. Dec. Officers' authority is limited by duty to safeguard government interests; extensions that prejudice the Government are improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension after completion with accrued liquidated damages requires new consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: When work is not completed until after the expiration of the period fixed in the contract and liquidated damages have accrued for the period of the delay, an extension of time cannot be granted after the expiration of such period and after completion and acceptance of the work without a new and adequate consideration, as it would operate as a release or waiver of liability for liquidated damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: XIII Comp. Dec. and related citations. Post-acceptance extensions that would waive accrued damages need fresh consideration; beware of retroactive waivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts to be strictly construed; relaxations irregular
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts once executed will be strictly construed, and no variation from standards or specifications will be permitted or authorized. If contract requirements are unreasonable or tests impractical, the contract must not be modified but may be annulled with approval and relet inviting competition with full disclosure of changed requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Order No. 167 (War Department, Oct. 10, 1905). Prefer annulment and re-bidding over unilateral relaxation to protect fairness among bidders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary external changes may justify release despite loss to Government
rubrics_metrics.description: Where pending the execution of a contract the tariff was changed so as to impose a heavy loss on the contractor if compelled to carry out his contract, it was held that the Secretary of War could release the contractor from his contract, although the effect would impose a pecuniary loss on the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 28 Op. Atty. Gen. Recognize narrow exceptions where extraordinary changed conditions make performance excessively burdensome; such exceptions are situational and limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot accept substandard article without new consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: To accept mineral oil which does not come up to the tests specified in the original contract is not authorized without a new consideration therefor, and changed financial condition of the section where the contract is to be performed furnishes no consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.26846 and related. Modifying acceptance of nonconforming goods requires consideration; cannot justify by local financial hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of liquidated damages vested in Congress absent interest to US
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision purporting to give the Secretary of War power to waive liquidated damages is inoperative and void unless, under the circumstances, it would be to the interest of the United States to waive such damages; the contracting officer and contractor have no power to vest such power without compensation — such power vests in Congress only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.22730 and related citations. Strict limits on delegation of waiver power for liquidated damages; check congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual approval/termination clauses benefit the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract contained a provision 'that this contract shall be subject to the approval of the Commissary General ... and be terminable at any time by him,' this provision was inserted for the benefit of the United States, and does not authorize terminating a contract against the interests of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.11259. Interpret such clauses as exercisable for government's protection, not to its detriment.

rubrics_metrics.name: State regulatory changes do not impair government contract obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretary of War was without authority to waive the rights of the United States acquired under the contract; and the Public Service Commission was without power to impair the obligation of a Government contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.29280. Government contracts are not subject to impairment by state regulatory approvals; federal contract obligations remain binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliveries apply to the contract under which they were accepted
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the same contractor had two contracts for furnishing hay, the prices being different, and hay had been ordered and delivered under the low-priced contract and payments had been made and accepted under the low-priced contract, deliveries could not subsequently be considered as made under the high-priced contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.21418. Acceptance and payment under a specific contract fixes application of deliveries; cannot reallocate deliveries to a different contract afterwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake that excludes true consent nullifies agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistake may be such that each party meant something different (their minds never met), so that the forms they have gone through are inoperative; such fundamental error nullifies the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Pollock on Contracts and multiple cases. Distinguish 'fundamental error' (voiding formation) from errors giving rise to equitable relief after formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bids containing clerical/typographical errors may be no bid at all if shown promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bidder made a clerical error in his bid (e.g., $4,350 instead of $9,350), the bid was held to be no bid at all and ought not to be considered; if accepted it would not be binding on the bidder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney General Miller (20 Op.) and other cases. Prompt notice and clear proof of clerical error before contractual acceptance are necessary to avoid binding obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief for serious mistake depends on promptness and clarity of error
rubrics_metrics.description: In Moffett, Hodgkins & Co. v. Rochester the court relieved bidder for a serious mistake by which an unreasonable low price was bid; the error was promptly availed of and the transaction had not reached the degree of a contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors: obviousness of error, prompt pursuit of remedy, whether acceptance had occurred, and whether 'minds met.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent fundamental errors known to government representatives allow bid withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bid was so clearly an error as to price that the error must have been known to the representatives of the Government, the bidder was entitled to withdraw his bid and it could not be properly accepted with knowledge of its being erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arctic overshoes (C.22558). If error is so marked that government should have noticed, acceptance is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidders may correct fundamental calculation errors with evidentiary proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A bidder should be required to clearly establish his error by evidence under oath, and also establish that the lead-pencil memorandum was the original estimate on which the bid was based; if shown, the bid may be reformed to reflect the real intention and include the same percentage of profit on the amount of the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.1654 and similar cases. Corrections allowed when supported by contemporaneous original estimates and sworn evidence; do not allow additional or new items not in original estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entering into contract with knowledge of one's bid error constitutes waiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Where through a clerical error a bidder proposed a price far below market, and with knowledge of the error entered into a contract and completed the same, the contractor by entering into the contract with knowledge of the error had waived it, and an additional price could not be paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.8942 and related. If bidder knows the mistake yet knowingly accepts the contract, relief is forfeited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales by both sample and description must conform to both
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a sale was by both sample and description, it was not sufficient that the goods delivered conformed to the sample; they must conform also to the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.4332, C.23732. In procurement specifying 'like sample' plus descriptive requirements, ensure delivered goods meet both criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors of unit/quantity ambiguity may render proposal non-binding
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bidder omits necessary specificity (e.g., bids for total quantity without naming size, or bids per pound instead of per unit), such mistakes may exclude true consent and the proposals containing erroneous prices should not be treated as binding upon the parties making them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.6802 and others. Ambiguous bids that do not clearly express intended offer can be disregarded as non-binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: If contract is based on mistake discovered after partial performance, it may be non-binding and remedies limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bidder offered mistakenly low price and a contract was entered and part supplies furnished, after discovery the contract was held not binding on the contractor; a supplemental contract could be made to pay for supplies already finished and contract with actual lowest bidder made for remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.20323 (bacon example). Remedies may include payment for work done and re-contracting for balance rather than specific performance at mistaken price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance location must conform to contract description
rubrics_metrics.description: When a contract provided for installing a wireless-telegraph system between two points, one described as 'at or near the mouth of Delta River and Bates Rapids,' the selection of a point 75 miles distant from the mouth did not comply with the terms of the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.12705. Material location/designation terms cannot be unilaterally altered by the government without contractor consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of site after contracting relieves contractor of obligation to new site
rubrics_metrics.description: Where after the contract had been signed the United States changed the site of the proposed quarters to a location about 450 feet from the original site, the contractor was under no legal obligation to carry out the contract on the new site, even though the new site was more advantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.20300. Alteration of a material term (site) requires agreement; contractor need not accept unilateral site changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for commencing manufacture may be extended if procurement impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: If investigation shows that it was a practical impossibility to procure the materials within the contract time for commencing manufacture, the time for commencing manufacture could lawfully be extended accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.22587 (canvas leggins example). Demonstrable practical impossibility to obtain specified materials justifies extension of commencement times.
